facts.text: Its wings are short and round, capable only of weak flight, mainly used for balance or gliding from trees to the ground.
facts.quote: The wings are short and round, and are only capable of weak flight, being mainly used for balance or for gliding from trees to the ground.

facts.text: Around 70–80% of a male's vocalisations are imitations of other species, mostly other birds but occasionally marsupials.
facts.quote: with an estimated 70–80% of the male's vocalisations consisting of imitations of other species, mostly other birds but occasionally marsupials.

facts.text: The mimicry is so accurate that shrike-thrushes in one study could not tell their own songs from lyrebird imitations of them.
facts.quote: one study found that shrike-thrushes did not respond any differently to hearing their own songs than to hearing imitations by lyrebirds.

facts.text: Males build several circular mounds of bare dirt on the forest floor and defend them vigorously for courtship displays.
facts.quote: Within his territory, the male will construct several circular mounds of bare dirt on the forest floor, for the purpose of conducting courtship displays.

facts.text: The female breeds once per year in winter, usually laying a single egg that is incubated for up to seven weeks.
facts.quote: The female breeds once per year in winter, usually laying a single egg. Eggs are laid in a deep bed of lyrebird feathers within the nest, and are then incubated by the female for up to 7 weeks.

facts.text: A single lyrebird can move and bury up to 200 tonnes of leaf litter and soil per hectare every year, helping reduce wildfire fuel.
facts.quote: A lyrebird can move and bury up to 200 tonnes per hectare of leaf litter and soil every year, disturbing the soil to a greater extent than virtually any other animal.

facts.text: A male superb lyrebird appears on the reverse side of the Australian 10-cent coin.
facts.quote: a male superb lyrebird being featured on the reverse side of the Australian 10-cent coin

facts.text: A male superb lyrebird reaches maturity in 7–9 years, while the female matures in 6–7 years.
facts.quote: The male superb lyrebird reaches maturity in 7–9 years, and the female in 6–7 years.

facts.text: The superb lyrebird's diet consists primarily of invertebrates such as earthworms and insects found on the forest floor.
facts.quote: The diet of the superb lyrebird consists primarily of invertebrates such as earthworms and insects found on the forest floor.

facts.text: The superb lyrebird lives in the forests of southeastern Australia, from southern Victoria to southeastern Queensland.
facts.quote: The superb lyrebird is found in the forests of southeastern Australia, ranging from southern Victoria to southeastern Queensland.
